exercises.video_explanation_script: Wrist curls are the foundational exercise for building bigger, stronger forearms. Sit on a bench and rest your forearms on your thighs with your wrists hanging off your knees. Hold a barbell with an underhand grip - palms facing up. Let your wrists extend back and the bar can even roll down to your fingertips for a full stretch. From here, curl your wrists up by flexing them, bringing your knuckles toward your forearms. Squeeze hard at the top. Your forearms never leave your thighs - only your wrists and hands move. Lower back down with control. Use relatively light weight and focus on higher reps - forearms respond better to volume than heavy weight. This builds the muscles on the palm side of your forearm that are crucial for grip strength.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Reverse wrist curls are crucial for balanced forearm development and preventing wrist issues like tennis elbow. Set up exactly like regular wrist curls - sit on a bench with your forearms resting on your thighs and wrists hanging off your knees. But this time, use an overhand grip with your palms facing down. Let your wrists flex down toward the floor. From here, extend your wrists by lifting the back of your hands up toward the sky. Squeeze your wrist extensors at the top. Lower back down with control. You'll use significantly less weight than regular wrist curls - maybe 30 to 50 percent less - and that's completely normal. The extensors on the back of your forearm are smaller and weaker than the flexors. These muscles are often neglected but they're essential for wrist health and complete forearm development.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Farmer's carries are one of the absolute best exercises for building crushing grip strength while also working your entire body. Stand between two heavy dumbbells or kettlebells and deadlift them up to a standing position. Hold them at your sides with your arms hanging straight down. Now here's what makes this effective: grip those handles as hard as you possibly can, like you're trying to crush them. Stand tall with your chest up and shoulders packed down - not shrugged up. Walk forward in a straight line with controlled, deliberate steps. Maintain that upright posture and tight grip the entire time. Walk until your grip starts to fail. This builds incredible grip strength, strengthens your traps, and challenges your entire core. The weight should be heavy enough that your grip is seriously challenged.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Dead hangs are one of the simplest yet most effective exercises for building grip strength. Find a pull-up bar and grab it with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder-width apart. Jump or step up so you're hanging with your arms fully extended and your feet off the ground. This is a dead hang - your arms are completely straight. Now just hang there and focus on maintaining your grip. Your shoulders should be slightly engaged, not fully relaxed and shrugged up to your ears. Breathe normally and grip the bar as tight as you can. Hang until your grip involuntarily fails and you have to let go. When you're starting out, even 10-20 seconds might be challenging, and that's fine. Work your way up. This builds incredible grip strength and endurance, plus it decompresses your spine and is great for shoulder health.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Plate pinches develop a specific type of grip strength - pinch grip - which is crucial for many real-world tasks and activities like rock climbing. Take two weight plates and pinch them together with the smooth sides facing out. Your fingers go on one side and your thumb goes on the other side. Lift the plates off the ground so you're holding them at your side with your arm hanging straight down. Now just hold this position, squeezing the plates together as hard as you can. Your thumb should be working incredibly hard. Hold until your grip fails and you have to let the plates drop. Start light - maybe two 10-pound plates or even a single 10-pound plate. Pinch grip is much weaker than your regular crushing grip. This type of grip strength is often neglected but it's incredibly important for complete grip development.

exercises.video_explanation_script: The wrist roller is an old-school forearm exercise that's incredibly effective. Hold the wrist roller bar with your arms extended straight out in front of you at shoulder height. A weight hangs below on a rope attached to the bar. Using an overhand grip, alternately roll your wrists to wind the rope around the bar, raising the weight. One wrist flexes while the other extends in a rolling motion. Keep your arms straight - don't bend your elbows. Roll until the weight reaches the bar. Then reverse the process, using your wrist extensors to control the weight back down. One complete cycle up and down is brutal but incredibly effective. Your shoulders will burn from holding your arms up - that's part of it. Start light, maybe 2.5 to 5 pounds, because this is much harder than it looks. This hits every muscle in your forearms.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Towel pull-ups are an advanced variation that builds incredible grip strength. Drape a towel over a pull-up bar and grab both ends of the towel in each hand - or use two towels, one for each hand. Hang with your arms fully extended. The towel is unstable and difficult to grip, which is the point. From this dead hang, pull yourself up just like a regular pull-up, but you have to maintain that crushing grip on the towel the entire time. Pull until your chin clears the bar, then lower under control. This is significantly harder than regular pull-ups - your grip will likely fail before your back does. You might only get a few reps at first, and that's completely normal. This variation is popular in martial arts and climbing training because it builds functional, real-world grip strength.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Zottman curls are a brilliant exercise that combines bicep and forearm training in one movement. Stand with dumbbells at your sides. Curl them up just like a regular bicep curl with your palms facing up. At the top of the movement, rotate your wrists so your palms are now facing down. Now lower the dumbbells with this overhand grip. This lowering phase with your palms down really hammers your forearm extensors - you'll feel it burning. At the bottom, rotate your wrists back to palms up and repeat. The underhand curl works your biceps, and the overhand lower works your forearms. You'll need to use lighter weight than standard curls because of that challenging lowering phase. This is one of the most efficient arm exercises you can do.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Hand gripper training is one of the most convenient ways to build crushing grip strength. You can get quality grippers like Captains of Crush in various resistance levels. Hold the gripper in one hand with the palm on one handle and your fingers on the other. From the open position, squeeze the gripper closed until the handles touch - that's a full close. Hold it for a second, then control it back open. The goal is always to achieve full closure where the handles touch. Don't get a gripper that's too hard - start with one you can close 5 to 10 times with perfect form. As you get stronger, progress to harder grippers. This type of crushing grip strength is incredibly functional and the gripper is so portable you can train anywhere. Close it for a few sets on each hand throughout the day.

exercises.video_explanation_script: Fat grip training is a simple but brutally effective way to build grip strength - just make the bar thicker. Fat Gripz are rubber attachments that increase any barbell to about 2 inches in diameter. Attach them to a barbell and perform standard barbell curls, but here's the catch: you'll need to reduce the weight by 20 to 30 percent or more because the thick bar is so much harder to grip. Set up like a regular barbell curl with your arms extended and elbows at your sides. As you curl, you'll notice your forearms working incredibly hard just to maintain your grip on that thick bar. Crush the bar as hard as you can throughout the entire set. Your grip will likely fatigue before your biceps, and that's exactly the point. This builds both your biceps and your grip strength simultaneously. You can apply Fat Gripz to any exercise - curls, rows, deadlifts - to make grip the limiting factor.
